items.title: You cannot walk across all seven Königsberg bridges once
items.claim: Königsberg (now Kaliningrad) sat on two riverbanks and two islands connected by seven bridges. The town's puzzle: is there a route that crosses each bridge exactly once? Euler proved in 1735 that there isn't — and invented graph theory in the process.
items.prompt: What's the criterion for the puzzle to have a solution?

options.text: Bridges must be arranged in a circle
Every vertex (landmass) must have even degree (an even number of bridges), except possibly the start and end points; Königsberg has four landmasses, all of odd degree
Bridges must be the same length

items.reveal_title: Euler's 1735 paper — birth of graph theory
items.reveal:
Euler abstracted Königsberg to a 'graph': landmasses become vertices, bridges become edges. The puzzle asks for an 'Eulerian path' (a walk using every edge exactly once).

Euler proved: an Eulerian path exists if and only if at most 2 vertices have odd degree. (A circuit, starting and ending at the same vertex, requires every vertex to have even degree.)

Königsberg: north bank had 3 bridges, south bank 3, east island 5, west island 3. All four are odd. So no Eulerian path exists.

Euler's paper was the first to study a problem in what we now call topology — caring about connections, not distances. Graph theory grew into a major branch of mathematics: shortest paths, network flows, Internet routing, social networks, and more.

Two of Königsberg's bridges were destroyed in World War II; only three of the original seven remain. Today the puzzle has a valid Eulerian path.
items.why: Geometric puzzles often look like they need detailed measurement. Sometimes only the abstract topology matters — and Euler's degree condition makes the answer trivial once formalised.

items.title: If something grows at 3% per year, it doubles in 23 years
items.claim: Compound growth at rate r% has a fixed doubling time of about 70/r years (rule of 70) or 72/r (rule of 72). The doubling time doesn't change as the quantity grows. That's what 'exponential' means — proportional rate, not larger jumps.
items.prompt: Why is the doubling time constant?

options.text: For exponential growth dN/dt = kN, N(t) = N0 * e^(kt). Doubling time T = ln(2)/k ≈ 0.693/k. Independent of N0 — the time to go from 1 to 2 equals the time to go from 1000 to 2000
Only applies to populations of bacteria

items.reveal:
Exponential growth: dN/dt = k * N. Solution: N(t) = N_0 e^(kt). Doubling time T = ln(2)/k.

Rule of 70/72: if k% per period, doubling time ≈ 70/k (or 72/k) periods. At 7%/year, doubles in ~10 years. At 1%/year, doubles in ~70 years. At 0.5%/year (current global population growth), doubles in ~140 years.

Exponential growth is unrealistic for long times — no real system maintains constant growth rate forever. The logistic model corrects: dN/dt = k * N * (1 - N/K), where K is the carrying capacity.

Logistic solution: N(t) = K / (1 + ((K - N_0)/N_0) * e^(-kt)). Starts exponential (when N << K), saturates at K.

Applications:
- Epidemics: early growth (susceptible >> infected) is exponential; saturates as susceptibles deplete (or interventions take effect). The famous 'flatten the curve' is intervening in this growth equation.
- Populations: many wild populations roughly logistic. Carrying capacity set by food, predation, disease.
- Innovation diffusion: technology adoption (smartphones, electric cars) often logistic.
- Tumour growth: early stages can be exponential; later stages limited by blood supply.

Misinterpretations:
- 'Exponential' is loosely used to mean 'fast growth'. Mathematically, it means proportional growth. A linear quantity can grow faster than an exponential one in the short term.
- Confusing exponential growth (rate proportional to value) with super-exponential (faster than any fixed exponential).
- Underestimating doubling times. Many people fail the 'penny doubling' problem: a penny doubled daily for 30 days becomes ~10 million dollars.
items.why: Exponential growth feels like 'fast growth'. Mathematically it's something specific: constant percentage rate, constant doubling time. Understanding doubling times is key to understanding epidemics, populations, finance, and Moore's law.

items.title: The simplest population equation in the world becomes chaotic
items.claim: Logistic map: x_(n+1) = r * x_n * (1 - x_n). At r = 2.5, x converges to a fixed point. At r = 3.2, it oscillates between two values. At r = 3.7, the values look random. The system is deterministic but unpredictable.

options.text: Nothing — the system is always periodic

Period-doubling cascade: a single fixed point splits into a 2-cycle, then a 4-cycle, then 8, 16, 32... at geometrically closer values of r (Feigenbaum's constant ~4.669). Beyond ~3.5699, the system becomes chaotic
Only mathematicians can see the difference
The chaos is a calculation error

items.reveal_title: Period doubling and the road to chaos
items.reveal:
The logistic map x_(n+1) = r * x_n * (1 - x_n) was introduced by Robert May (1976) as a simple model of population growth with carrying capacity.

For r between 0 and 1: x converges to 0.
For r between 1 and 3: x converges to a non-zero fixed point.
At r = 3: the fixed point becomes unstable; period-2 cycle appears.
At r ≈ 3.449: period-4 cycle appears.
At r ≈ 3.544: period-8.
At r ≈ 3.5644: period-16.

The period-doublings occur at geometrically closer r-values, with ratio approaching Feigenbaum's constant delta ≈ 4.669 — a universal constant of period-doubling bifurcations, appearing in many physical systems (dripping faucet, electronic circuits, fluid dynamics).

At r ≈ 3.5699: 'Edge of chaos'. Beyond this, the system becomes chaotic — small differences in initial conditions grow exponentially.

Within the chaos there are 'islands of stability' (e.g., a period-3 window near r ≈ 3.83). The bifurcation diagram has fractal structure.

This system shows that deterministic dynamics can produce apparent randomness. It motivated chaos theory in the 1970s-80s.

Applications:
- Population biology (when not too realistic).
- Cryptography (pseudo-random number generators).
- Modelling complex systems (transitions to turbulence).
- Analogies to neural and economic dynamics.

The logistic map is a foundational example in the study of dynamical systems and has become a textbook reference for chaos.
items.why: Even the simplest equations can produce unpredictable behaviour. Determinism doesn't guarantee predictability — chaos can emerge from one-line iterations. This insight overturned 19th-century certainty about Newtonian mechanics.
